passages.happening:
The prophet praises God. “O LORD, You are my God! I will exalt You; I will praise Your name.” (verse 1). God has done wonders, plans formed long ago, in perfect faithfulness.

He has made the fortified city a heap of rubble; the fortress of strangers will never be rebuilt (verse 2). So a strong people will honor him, and the cities of ruthless nations will revere him (verse 3).

‘For You have been a refuge for the poor, a stronghold for the needy in distress, a refuge from the storm, a shade from the heat’ (verse 4). The breath of the ruthless is like rain against a wall. As the shade of a cloud cools the heat, ‘so the song of the ruthless is silenced’ (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 24 ended with the LORD reigning on Mount Zion after judging the earth. Chapter 25 shows what that reign looks like.

Like the rest of chapters 24 to 27, this chapter names no king or date. Those who hold that Isaiah wrote it point to its links with his earlier promise that the nations would stream to the mountain of the LORD. Those who date the section after the exile see the ruined city as a city of the Persian or early Greek world. As in chapter 24, the city is not named, and the praise is for a pattern of God's action as much as for one event.

The ruthless are loud, like a storm beating on a wall, and the poor are exposed, like people in the desert heat. God is both shelter and shade. The first hearers, who knew what the ruthless could do, were given a song about the God who sides with the needy.
passages.later: A psalm praises the same God: ‘You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies’ (Psalm 23:5).
passages.asks: God is called a refuge for the poor and a shade from the heat. Ask who around you is caught in the storm of someone else's ruthlessness. And ask whether you can be shade for them, as God is.

passages.t: A feast for all peoples, and death swallowed up
passages.happening:
‘On this mountain the LORD of Hosts will prepare a banquet for all the peoples, a feast of aged wine, of choice meat, of finely aged wine’ (verse 6).

‘On this mountain He will swallow up the shroud that enfolds all peoples, the sheet that covers all nations’ (verse 7). ‘He will swallow up death forever. The Lord GOD will wipe away the tears from every face and remove the disgrace of His people from the whole earth. For the LORD has spoken’ (verse 8).

In that day people will say, ‘Surely this is our God; we have waited for Him, and He has saved us’ (verse 9). This is the LORD they waited for; they will rejoice in his salvation.
passages.hearers:
The same mountain where the kings of the earth were humbled becomes the place where all nations eat together at God's table. This is one of the widest windows in the Old Testament onto God's purpose for the nations. Not only Israel but all the peoples are invited, and the enemy removed is not a nation but death itself.

A feast was the ancient world's picture of joy and plenty. Aged wine and rich food were what kings served at the great banquets. Here God is the host, and the guest list is every people.

The shroud over all peoples is the covering of grief, the cloth laid over the dead. God swallows it. In Canaanite stories the god of death was pictured as swallowing his victims. Here the LORD swallows death.

The first hearers had waited a long time. The words ‘we have waited for Him’ (verse 9) are the words of people whose patience has been answered.
passages.later: Paul quotes verse 8 for the resurrection of the body: ‘Death has been swallowed up in victory’ (1 Corinthians 15:54). Revelation takes up the promise twice: ‘God will wipe away every tear from their eyes’ (Revelation 7:17), and ‘there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain’ (Revelation 21:4).
passages.hard:
Does this chapter really teach the end of death, or is it a poetic way of describing national restoration?

Interpreters differ. Some read verse 8 as a vivid picture of the end of Israel's national humiliation, the death of exile and defeat, in the way Ezekiel 37 uses dry bones to picture Israel's return. Others argue that the language goes beyond metaphor: the tears are wiped from every face, the covering over all nations is removed, and death is swallowed forever, which suggests the end of death itself. Many scholars see this chapter, with 26:19 and Daniel 12:2, as a key stage in the Old Testament's growing hope of resurrection.

These readings need not exclude each other. The prophet may have seen Israel's restoration as the first part of a larger undoing of death. The New Testament reads verse 8 as a promise about bodily resurrection, and the church confesses that promise on the ground of Christ's own resurrection.

Grief is not a lack of faith. If your grief is so heavy that you cannot carry it, please tell someone: a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: God promises to wipe away the tears from every face. Ask whose tears you are waiting for God to wipe away, perhaps your own. And ask what it means that the guest list for God's feast is all the peoples.

passages.t: Moab, too proud for the feast
passages.happening:
‘For the hand of the LORD will rest on this mountain. But Moab will be trampled in his place as straw is trodden into the dung pile’ (verse 10).

He will spread out his hands in it, as a swimmer spreads his arms to swim, ‘His pride will be brought low, despite the skill of his hands’ (verse 11). ‘The high-walled fortress will be brought down, cast to the ground, into the dust’ (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
Moab, the kingdom east of the Dead Sea, was a related people and a long rival. Isaiah had already given two chapters to Moab, and here it becomes the example of the proud nation that refuses the feast. Its high-walled fortresses on the plateau east of the Jordan were famous for their strength.

The picture is harsh and earthy, a man struggling in a dung pile as a swimmer struggles in water. Moab's pride is its downfall. The feast is offered to all, and Moab stands outside because it will not come down.

As in the earlier oracles, Moab here is the ancient nation of Isaiah's day. The verses are not a key for naming any people now.
passages.later: Isaiah had already said, ‘We have heard of Moab’s pomposity, his exceeding pride and conceit’ (Isaiah 16:6), and Jeremiah repeats it (Jeremiah 48:29).
passages.asks: Moab is pictured outside the feast because of its pride. Ask whether pride is keeping you outside something God offers. And ask what it would mean for you to come to the table as a guest, not as a fortress.
